title: The price of lettuce
hookLine: someone else got invited: they paid the price in flattery, and you kept your coin (Enchiridion 25)

cards: The group photo goes up and you're not in it, because you weren't invited. Or the promotion goes to the person who laughs at all the boss's jokes and stays for every after-work drink.
Or the dinner party is next Saturday, and somehow your name didn't make the list. There's a sting, and right behind it a question: why them and not me?
In the handbook, Epictetus answers with a trip to the market, to the vegetable stall, where a head of lettuce costs one small coin.

teach.b: Someone was preferred to you, Epictetus says, at a dinner, or in being greeted, or in being asked for advice. If those are good things, be glad for them. If they're bad, don't be sorry they didn't come to you.
Then the market. How much is lettuce sold for? An obol, a small coin.
Someone pays the obol and takes the lettuce. You don't pay, and you don't take it. Are you worse off than the buyer?
He has the lettuce. You have the obol you didn't spend. So it is here, he says.
You weren't invited to someone's dinner? You didn't pay the host what the dinner sells for.
And the price is praise, and attention, and hanging around his doors, and putting up with his rudeness. If it's worth it to you, pay the price and go.
But if you want the dinner without paying, you're being greedy and foolish. And you haven't come away with nothing. You didn't praise someone you didn't want to praise.
You didn't put up with their insolence at the door. That's the coin in your pocket. It doesn't mean every invitation is bought with flattery; many are just friendship.
But when someone gets ahead by paying a price you chose not to pay, notice the coin you kept.
A look back at a week of steady footing: not my contest, the insult, nothing to envy, laughed at, keep your footing, faithful and modest, and the lettuce.

how: Some Stoic practitioners, when passed over, ask what price the other person paid and remind themselves of what they kept by not paying it.

o: a fee paid to a host to get a dinner invite
a small offering left at a temple for luck
a small Greek coin, the price of a lettuce

games.q: the price of lettuce — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says every invitation is bought with flattery
his point is about when a price was paid that you chose not to pay.
he says if the dinner is worth it to you, pay the price and go
but don't want it without paying.
an obol was a small Greek coin
the price of a head of lettuce in his example.

games.q: you weren't invited to the host's dinner. you never flattered him. what does Epictetus say you have?
o: the coin you didn't spend: no false praise, no insolence endured.
games.why: he has the dinner; you have what you didn't pay: you didn't praise whom you didn't want to, or put up with his insolence.

practice: Think of one thing someone else got that you didn't, an invitation, a role, a seat at a table, and let the sting come.
Then ask Epictetus' market question, what did it cost, and name the price honestly, if there was one: flattery, late nights, keeping quiet.
Put your hand on your pocket and name the coin you kept: your time, your honesty, your evening.

wordCard.voice: Obol. The small coin that buys the lettuce in Epictetus' market lesson: everything has a price; if someone paid it and you didn't, they have the lettuce, and you have the coin. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: I kept the coin. Another week of steady footing, done. See you tomorrow.
